title: The 1944 film Tunisian Victory re-created scenes after much American footage sank at sea
body: *Tunisian Victory* (1944) is the joint British–American documentary of the war in Tunisia. British army filmmakers, who had made the hit *Desert Victory* about El Alamein, were making their own film, *Africa Freed*; then the British and American wartime information agencies agreed on one joint film. Hollywood director Frank Capra, a US Army colonel, and Britain's Hugh Stewart, who led a joint staff of some 300 including 50 cameramen, made it. Much American footage was lost when German forces sank the ship carrying it, so scenes were re-created: George Stevens filmed tanks and troops for two weeks, and John Huston shot planes and dummy tanks in Orlando and the California desert; the [AFI Catalog](https://catalog.afi.com/Film/27693-TUNISIAN-VICTORY) is unsure those reached the final cut. After a months-long struggle over who would tell the story, Capra took control, and the film opened on 16 March 1944, as the [US National Archives](https://unwritten-record.blogs.archives.gov/2017/11/08/tunisian-victory-operation-torch-gets-the-hollywood-treatment) recounts. Britain's Imperial War Museum notes that it gives the American effort far more weight than *Africa Freed*.

slides.question: The fighting in Tunisia ended on 13 May 1943. How many months later did the Allied documentary Tunisian Victory open?
slides.explanation: About 10 months: it opened on 16 March 1944, after a long dispute between British and American officials over who would tell the story.

slides.alt: Animation in a dark cutting room: film cans for Desert Victory and Africa Freed, London and Washington agreeing on one film, cameras along a 2,000-mile front, a ship sinking with its reels, dummy tanks being filmed, two soldiers' voices, a tilted balance and a calendar to 16 March 1944.

slides.prompt: Set the running time of the finished film and see how much of the footage shot it keeps. Find the real length: 76 minutes.
slides.takeaway: 76 minutes is about 6,840 feet of film (the print measures 6,871): roughly one foot kept for every 44 shot, about 2% of the 300,000 feet Variety reported. The rest went unused here.

slides.heading: Who made it
items: Frank Capra: Hollywood director, US Army colonel
Hugh Stewart: British army film officer, led the team
George Stevens, John Huston: re-created scenes
Bernard Miles, Burgess Meredith: two soldiers’ voices
William Alwyn, Dimitri Tiomkin: the music

slides.heading: Filmed in the war, or made after?

left.label: From the campaign
left.text: Film shot by about 50 British and American cameramen on a 2,000-mile front, plus newsreels and captured enemy film.

right.label: Made afterwards
right.text: Re-created scenes, some shot by George Stevens, perhaps more by John Huston in Florida and California, and two invented soldiers.

slides.question: Why did the makers of the 1944 documentary Tunisian Victory re-create scenes of the campaign?
options: Much American footage sank at sea
They ran out of film stock
slides.explanation: German forces sank the ship carrying much of the American footage, says the US National Archives, so Frank Capra turned to stock footage and re-creations.

source.label: US National Archives, The Unwritten Record: Tunisian Victory, Operation Torch gets the Hollywood treatment
